title: 'Someone else will do it for less': Refugees in Kenya are powering tech for dwindling pay
key_facts: Refugees in Kakuma camp in Kenya do remote digital tasks for tech companies, such as data annotation, translation and research, often through anonymous microwork platforms.
AOP Connect, a research platform owned by RWS (a British AI enterprise software company), offers 'discretionary rewards' of up to $500 instead of guaranteed wages.
Remotasks, a Scale AI subsidiary, left Kenya in 2024; workers had earned about $3 to $6 a day before that.
The International Trade Centre estimates jobs such as transcription, data entry, translation and web research have declined by about 50% since 2022.
Refugee workers say that as AI speeds up their work, their billable time and pay are falling; one provider says clients now threaten to hire someone who can do a job in two hours.
RWS says AOP Connect does not offer data annotation work; Scale AI did not respond to the broader findings.
quote_evidence: The language of ‘rewards’ instead of wages shifts risk entirely on to workers, who invest their time and expertise without any guarantee of fair compensation,
“We used to get three to five jobs per month,” he said. “Now you cannot get one.”
why_it_matters_hint: AI is shrinking the low-paid digital jobs that refugees relied on, while the data work underpins AI tools.
notes: Read in full (Guardian, 13,895 characters). Interviews with more than two dozen refugees and organisations, plus documents seen by the Guardian. Pay figures for AOP rewards are described as the listing amount, not guaranteed wages.
